citation: Newman, D., Finney, P. B., Bell, S., Turner, H., Jaciw, A. P., Zacamy, J. L., & Gould, L. F. (2012). Evaluation of the Effectiveness of the Alabama Math, Science, and Technology Initiative (AMSTI). Final Report. (NCEE 2012-4008). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. Prepared by Empirical Education Inc. and the Regional Educational Laboratory Southeast.
design: Cluster-randomized controlled trial; unit of assignment = School (matched pairs of schools randomly assigned within pair to AMSTI vs business-as-usual control). 82 schools (~780 teachers, ~30,000 students) across two pooled subexperiments (40 schools randomized winter 2006, 42 schools winter 2007), grades 4-8 in Alabama, low-income/high-minority sample. Single TPD arm: AMSTI = teacher professional development (summer PD, access to materials/manipulatives, in-school support) for math and science. Subjects: mathematics (SAT 10 math problem solving, grades 4-8) and science (SAT 10 science, grades 5 & 7 only). Impact estimates from a benchmark multilevel (HLM) model with matched-pair fixed effects, pretest and demographic covariates -> accounts for school clustering and adjusts for pretest. Grade = Mixed (4-8).
problems: (1) The ONLY uncontaminated TPD-vs-business-as-usual contrast is the ONE-YEAR effect: the control group entered AMSTI in Year 2, so it was no longer a pure control, and the report itself labels the two-year impacts exploratory (computed with extra assumptions). I therefore extract the one-year confirmatory math and science effects (the report's headline outcomes) plus the one-year exploratory reading effect; the two-year exploratory results (math g~0.10, science g~0.13) are NOT extracted as primary contrasts and are described in notes only. (2) The report's own effect sizes (math 0.05, science 0.05, reading 0.06) are computed as regression-adjusted impact / SD of the control-group POSTTEST (with between-grade variance factored out of the denominator). I reproduce these by standardizing each impact estimate by the reported control-group posttest SD (math 42.4, science 31.3, reading 36.8); the resulting g matches the report's rounded ES exactly, so the standardizing SD is well identified. (3) g is computed from the multilevel impact coefficient and its model-based SE, which already account for school-level clustering, so cluster_adjusted=true and g_se = J*(impact_se/SD_control); a separate design-effect ICC is not reported (NOT guessed). (4) SAT 10 is a standardized/independent norm-referenced state-accountability assessment (test_type=standardized_independent). (5) Although the registry tags this study Low SES and the population is predominantly free/reduced-price-lunch eligible, the extracted effects are for the FULL analytic sample (is_full_sample=true); the report's FRL-eligibility, minority, gender, and pretest subgroup analyses found no significant differential effects and are not extracted as separate subgroup rows. (6) The unadjusted posttest means in the descriptive tables (Tables 4.1, 4.3, 6.1) actually slightly favor the control group; the regression-adjusted (covariate-adjusted) model reverses this to favor AMSTI, which is why mean_t here is the reported AMSTI mean = control unadjusted mean + adjusted impact (Tables 4.2, 4.4, 6.2), not the raw unadjusted AMSTI mean.

Two-year exploratory effect (control no longer pure) was 3.74 scale points, SE 1.66, ES 0.10, p=.030 (Table 5.2) -- NOT extracted here per spec (use end-of-pure-control wave = Year 1).
